strengths: Addresses a meaningful and timely task — temporally consistent street-view video generation from a single satellite image along a trajectory — that goes beyond existing one-to-one cross-view image synthesis.

The two proposed components are well motivated: ray-based pixel attention over a tri-plane representation injects explicit cross-view geometry into the diffusion conditioning, and epipolar-constrained temporal attention leverages known relative poses to restrict cross-frame attention, reducing complexity from O(NHW × NHW) to O(NHW × NM).

Introduces VIGOR++, a large-scale benchmark (~90k satellite–ground video pairs, 10 cities) with trajectory annotations, which is a valuable community resource given the lack of cross-view video datasets.

Fairly comprehensive evaluation protocol combining perceptual, semantic, pixel-wise, depth-consistency, and temporal metrics, plus a downstream application (cross-view localization with G2SWeakly) demonstrating practical utility of the generated data.
Includes useful ablations: single-image setting isolating the cross-view conditioning module (Table 2), epipolar vs. full cross attention (Table 4), and memory scaling analysis (Figure 7).
weaknesses: Key technical claims are under-specified. The paper claims the tri-plane 'encodes scene geometry directly from the satellite image' without height maps, but it is unclear how metric height information along the XZ/YZ planes is learned from a single top-down image with no 3D supervision; details are deferred to an appendix that is not included in the submission. The incremental refinement loop (projecting synthesized frames back into the tri-plane) is also only sketched.

Metric reporting raises validity concerns: Table 1 reports FVD values of ~2.1 and CLIPSIM of ~6.8, which are far outside the typical ranges for these metrics (FVD is usually in the hundreds; CLIPSIM is typically 0.2–0.3), and the units/normalization of the Depth metric are never defined. Without clarification, the quantitative claims are hard to interpret or trust.

Baseline coverage for the main task is weak: all three baselines (Sat2Density, ControlS2S, EscherNet) are single-image or general multi-view methods adapted to the video setting, and the most directly relevant prior video work [50] is excluded. This makes the headline comparison somewhat favorable and the true state-of-the-art positioning unclear.

Novelty is incremental: ray-based feature sampling resembles existing geometry-guided cross-view conditioning, the tri-plane representation and CVHA are adopted from prior work ([14], [26]), and epipolar-constrained attention builds on epipolar transformers and Tune-A-Video-style temporal attention. The contribution is a reasonable integration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The VIGOR++ construction process (semi-automatic path extraction via sky-color histograms and embedding similarity, then manual refinement) is described only at a high level; the quality, temporal coherence, and temporal gaps of the resulting 'video' sequences stitched from independently captured Street View panoramas are not analyzed, which matters since the model is trained to match these as temporally coherent video.

Ablations are incomplete: no ablation of tri-plane vs. BEV representation, the number of sampled depths K / attention heads J, the sparse two-previous-frames strategy, or DDIM steps; no user study; no evaluation of generalization to unseen cities despite the dataset claiming disjoint train/test locations.

Reproducibility and ethics gaps: no code or dataset release statement, no discussion of Google Maps/Street View licensing and terms-of-service constraints for the VIGOR++ data, and no quantification of dataset construction cost/consistency.

strengths: The task setting is practically relevant and relatively underexplored: generating temporally coherent ground-view video from a single satellite image and a 4-DoF trajectory is a meaningful step beyond single-image cross-view synthesis.

The two proposed modules (ray-based pixel attention over a tri-plane representation, and epipolar-constrained temporal attention) are conceptually reasonable and reduce the reliance on handcrafted projections or height maps.
The paper introduces VIGOR++, a new large-scale benchmark (90k+ satellite-ground video pairs, 10 cities) for cross-view video generation, which could benefit the community.
Evaluation covers a broad set of metrics (perceptual, semantic, pixel-level, depth consistency, FVD/CLIPSIM) and includes a downstream cross-view localization application.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely a recombination of existing components (tri-plane from EG3D, CVHA from BEVFormer, deformable attention, Stable Diffusion 1.5 finetuning, sparse temporal attention). The epipolar-constrained temporal attention is the most original piece, but its formulation (Eq. 6-7) is thin and the claimed advantage over standard temporal attention is not rigorously analyzed beyond one ablation.

The most directly comparable prior work, the satellite-to-ground video method of Xu & Qin [50], is excluded from comparison, with only 'code unavailable' as justification; given it is the closest related setting, the authors should reimplement or adapt it. Baselines on the video task (Sat2Density, ControlS2S, EscherNet) are image-level methods that are structurally disadvantaged, weakening the claimed superiority.

Technical description is too vague to be reproducible: key details (deformable attention offsets, K sampled depths, tri-plane resolution, the incremental projection-refinement loop, Eq. 3 notation) are deferred to a nonexistent-in-main-paper appendix or left undefined; the claimed M << HW complexity reduction is asserted without analysis of how candidate epipolar points are actually selected.

Some evaluation choices are questionable: the reported gains in Table 1 are modest and the paper itself concedes pixel-level metrics are unreliable, yet SSIM/PSNR improvements are still presented as evidence; the downstream localization improvement (5.22 -> 4.99) is small with no statistical significance; no user study or human evaluation is provided despite the generative nature of the task.

The VIGOR++ dataset construction (semi-automatic path extraction via sky color histograms and embedding similarity, followed by 'manual refinement') is under-specified, and the use of Google Maps/Street View data raises licensing and redistribution concerns that are not addressed.

Missing important related baselines in the video setting (e.g., Streetscapes [8], Skyeyes [11], CrossViewDiff [23]) and missing ablations on key hyperparameters (number of sampled points, tri-plane resolution, number of context frames), which limits the strength of the empirical claims.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and relatively underexplored task: temporally consistent ground-view video generation from a single satellite image and a trajectory, with a clear motivation for simulation, autonomous driving, and digital twin applications.

The two proposed technical components are well-motivated: the tri-plane scene representation with ray-based pixel attention provides a principled way to establish satellite-to-ground correspondences without height maps, and the epipolar-constrained temporal attention injects geometric priors into temporal consistency modeling while reducing computational cost.

The paper introduces VIGOR++, a large-scale benchmark (~90k satellite–ground video pairs across 10 cities) with trajectory annotations, which is a valuable community resource for cross-view video generation.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: comparisons on VIGOR++ for the video task, plus single-image comparisons on CVUSA and VIGOR against multiple published baselines (Pix2Pix, S2S, Sat2Density, ControlNet, ControlS2S), covering perceptual, semantic, pixel-level, depth, and temporal metrics.

Includes ablations for both key modules (Table 4 for epipolar vs. full cross-attention; tri-plane conditioning isolated via the single-image setting), a memory/efficiency analysis (Figure 7), and a downstream cross-view localization experiment demonstrating practical utility of the synthetic data.
weaknesses: The most relevant prior work on satellite-to-ground video generation [50] is excluded from comparison due to unavailability of code/data, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art video generation; the adapted EscherNet baseline is a generic multi-view model and is not a strong video-generation competitor.

Potential metric reporting issues: Table 1 marks CLIPSIM with a down arrow, but frame-to-frame CLIP similarity is conventionally higher-is-better; under that convention ControlS2S (6.651) would beat the proposed method (5.623). This inconsistency needs clarification and undermines confidence in the reported temporal-consistency gains.

The claimed novelty is incremental in places: the framework assembles known techniques (tri-plane representation, CVHA, deformable attention, epipolar geometry constraints, SD 1.5 finetuning); the key differentiator vs. ControlS2S in the single-image setting is essentially a scene representation swap, and the ablation does not fully disentangle tri-plane from ray-based attention contributions.

Generation resolution is limited (128×512) and no results at higher resolution or comparisons of compute cost vs. baselines are provided; long-range trajectory generation quality and drift behavior over long sequences are not quantitatively analyzed.

VIGOR++ construction relies on semi-automatic trajectory extraction from Google Street View with manual refinement; details on annotation quality control, licensing/redistribution implications, and a commitment to public release are not provided, which affects reproducibility.
Results are reported without variance or statistical significance, several FID/PSNR margins over ControlS2S are modest, and there is no human evaluation to corroborate the perceptual claims.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and relatively underexplored task: generating multiview-consistent 360° ground-level panorama sequences from a single satellite image along a trajectory, going beyond prior single-frame satellite-to-ground synthesis.

Technically well-motivated design: the triplane scene representation with ray-based pixel attention provides explicit cross-view geometric conditioning without requiring height maps, and the panoramic epipolar-constrained attention extends epipolar priors from pinhole to equirectangular imagery, with a clean geometric derivation provided in the appendix.

Introduces VIGOR++, a large-scale benchmark (~90k satellite–ground video pairs, 10 cities, train/test split from disjoint locations) that fills a real gap in the community and can serve future work in cross-view sequence synthesis and 3D reconstruction.

Evaluation is broad: single-frame comparisons on CVUSA and VIGOR against multiple baselines, sequence-level metrics (FVD, CLIPSIM), a novel geometric consistency evaluation via feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3DPS/3DSS), extensive ablations (triplane vs. BEV, ray attention vs. standard cross-attention, dynamic offset refinement, sparse vs. dense interframe attention), and a downstream cross-view localization application demonstrating practical utility.

Clear writing overall with an overview figure, honest limitations section (near-pose duplication artifacts, slow inference, dataset coverage constraints), and a reproducibility statement promising code and dataset release.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage for the main sequence-generation task is thin and somewhat indirect: EscherNet is a general object-level multiview model adapted to this setting, Sat2Density is not designed for sequence consistency, and the closest related systems (Streetscapes/Xu & Qin 2025, Deng et al. 2024) are excluded due to unavailable code/data. This weakens the claim of state-of-the-art multiview generation, though the exclusion rationale is stated.

Metric reporting is unclear and potentially misleading: FVD values around 2.1 and CLIPSIM around 6.8 are far outside conventional ranges for these metrics, with no explanation of normalization or computation; similarly 'DINO', 'Depth', 'Palexp/Psqueeze', and 'LRCE' are used without precise definitions. This makes cross-paper comparability impossible and raises concerns about metric validity.

Quantitative margins over ControlS2S in Table 1, while consistent, are moderate on several metrics (e.g., SegAny 0.3964 vs. 0.3718; SSIM 0.3964 vs. 0.3718), and some single-frame results in Table 2 (e.g., SD, DINO on CVUSA) show Ours slightly behind baselines on some columns, suggesting the advantage is not uniform.

Novelty is incremental in places: the triplane representation, deformable/ray-based sampling, and epipolar-constrained attention all adapt existing components (CVHA, triplane diffusion, Epidiff/Re-MVS style epipolar attention) to the panoramic cross-view setting; the panoramic epipolar derivation is straightforward given the equirectangular projection model.

Dataset construction relies on Google Maps/Street View imagery and semi-automatic trajectory harvesting; licensing and redistribution constraints for VIGOR++ are not addressed, and broader-impact discussion of scraping legal issues is absent despite a social-impact section.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming (SatDreamer360 vs. SatDream360), several typos ('mutiview', 'Epipolar-Attt'), citations formatted as 'goo (a)'/'goo (b)', and key architectural details deferred to the appendix, making the main text harder to assess.

Some claimed efficiency/consistency benefits rely on design choices (e.g., attending only to the two preceding frames) that also cap long-range consistency; long-sequence (>5 frame) quality beyond memory curves is not quantitatively evaluated.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and relatively unexplored task: trajectory-controlled, multiview-consistent 360° ground-view generation from a single satellite image, going beyond single-image cross-view synthesis.
Introduces VIGOR++, a large-scale dataset (~90k cross-view satellite/ground-video pairs across 10 cities) that could benefit future work on cross-view sequence synthesis and localization.

Covers both cross-view geometric conditioning (triplane + ray-based attention) and inter-frame consistency (panoramic epipolar attention), with several ablation studies (scene representation, attention design, sparse inter-frame strategy, dynamic offset refinement) and a downstream localization experiment.

The panoramic epipolar constraint derivation (Appendix A.3) is a reasonable geometric extension of epipolar attention from pinhole to equirectangular images, and the complexity analysis for the sparse inter-frame strategy is informative.
weaknesses: Serious concerns about the validity of the evaluation metrics. Several reported values appear inconsistent with established scales: FVD of ~2.1 is implausibly low for video generation (typical values are orders of magnitude larger), and CLIPSIM of 6.82 does not match the usual [0,1] CLIP similarity range. Metrics such as 'Palex', 'Psqueeze', 'SD', 'Depth', and 'LRCE' are never precisely defined (directions of improvement, normalization, units), making the main results (Tables 1 and 2) difficult to interpret or trust.

Weak and potentially unfair baselines. Only three baselines are compared, all retrained on the authors' own new dataset. EscherNet is an object-centric method adapted to an out-of-domain setting, and ControlS2S is designed for single-image generation; the most relevant recent works for continuous generation (Xu & Qin 2025, Deng et al. 2024) are excluded because code is unavailable. The claimed SOTA on VIGOR++ is therefore weakly supported.

Limited technical novelty. The framework is largely an assembly of existing components: triplane representations, CVHA cross-view hybrid attention, deformable-attention-based ray feature sampling, and epipolar-constrained attention from prior work (Tseng et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2024), with the main new element being the adaptation of epipolar attention to equirectangular panoramas.

Dataset construction raises reproducibility and licensing concerns. VIGOR++ is built from Google Maps/Street View with a 'semi-automatic' pipeline (sky histograms, embedding similarity, DFS path extraction plus manual refinement) that is described too briefly to reproduce; terms of use for derived Street View sequences are not addressed. Code and data are only 'promised', not released.

Some claims are overstated or sloppily written (e.g., 'To obtain the optimal solution for ground image inference'), typos persist ('mutiview', 'Epipolar-Attt'), and qualitative comparisons rely on small, cherry-picked trajectory examples with limited scene diversity.

The paper does not analyze failure modes or generalization quantitatively on the held-out cities (no per-city breakdown), and the<8m frame duplication artifact is only discussed after acceptance-relevant experiments are done.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and relatively unexplored problem: generating multiview-consistent 360-degree ground panoramas from a single satellite image along a trajectory, which prior cross-view generation work largely does not handle.

The technical design is well-motivated: the triplane scene representation with ray-based pixel attention provides explicit cross-view geometric grounding without requiring height maps, and the epipolar-constrained attention is a sensible extension of pose-guided consistency mechanisms from pinhole imagery to equirectangular panoramas, with a clean geometric derivation in the appendix.
Introduces VIGOR++, a substantial new benchmark (90k+ cross-view satellite/ground-video pairs across 10 cities with trajectories), which is a valuable community contribution beyond the method itself.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against retrained baselines on the new dataset (Table 1), standard single-image comparisons on CVUSA/VIGOR (Table 2), multiple ablations (triplane vs. BEV, ray-based vs. standard cross-attention, dynamic offset refinement, sparse vs. dense interframe attention) including efficiency analyses, plus a downstream localization application that demonstrates practical utility.

Good reproducibility posture: detailed training protocol (Appendix A.5), promise to release code and dataset, and an honest limitations section (e.g., <8m pose-spacing artifacts, slow inference, dataset coverage constraints).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: triplane representations, deformable/ray sampling, and epipolar-constrained attention all exist in prior work (Chan et al., Tseng et al., CVHA from Li et al.); the contribution is largely a careful combination and adaptation to the panoramic satellite-to-ground setting rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Some evaluation metrics are questionable or non-standard. FVD values of ~2-11 (Table 1) are implausibly low compared to typical video generation literature, raising concerns about how FVD was computed (sample size, frame count). 'Palex'/'Psqueeze' (AlexNet/SqueezeNet features) and DINO/SegAny as 'semantic level' metrics are unconventional and their exact protocol is under-specified, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable.

Key direct competitors (Xu & Qin 2025; Deng et al. 2024) are excluded from comparison due to unreleased code/data. While the justification is reasonable, this means the central claim of outperforming the most relevant state of the art in sequence generation rests on weaker, adapted baselines (Sat2Density, EscherNet, ControlS2S).

'Ours' wins on every single metric in every table, which is atypical; combined with non-standard metrics, some skepticism is warranted about metric design favoring the proposed method. Pixel-level metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are acknowledged by the authors to be poorly suited to this one-to-many generation task, yet are still reported prominently.

Table 2 shows the method is clearly worse on some metrics relative to specific baselines on VIGOR single-image generation (e.g., SegAny 0.3471 vs. Sat2Density's 0.3627), but the narrative claims superiority broadly; the discussion of metric trade-offs is uneven.

The dataset construction relies on semi-automatic path extraction with manual refinement; the curation protocol, quality control statistics, and license/redistribution terms for Google Maps/Street View data (a potential legal/ethical issue) are not sufficiently detailed.

Scaling to large scenes (Appendix A.4) is handled by incremental triplane updates, but this is demonstrated only qualitatively (Figure 9) with no quantitative evaluation of long-sequence or multi-batch consistency.
